newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH ANALYSTS SAY UNPLUG CEZ SHARES.
newsitem.headline: CZECH ANALYSTS SAY UNPLUG CEZ SHARES.

text.p: Shares in the main Czech power producer, CEZ a.s. , are overvalued at current levels and should be sold, analysts said on Monday.

Shares of CEZ, which supplies about 75 percent of the country's power, lost six crowns on Monday to 925. Some analysts said the stock would only become attractive at more than 100 crowns lower due to a decline in power use.
"We recommend to sell CEZ shares and consider buying under the 800 level," said Pavel Capouch of Stratego Invest.

CEZ had to slash its profit forecast to between five and six billion crowns this year from original estimates of 6.1 billion crowns due to a fall in demand. Last year the firm's net profit dropped to 7.8 billion from 8.1 billion in 1995.
Demand fell 5.5 percent in the first quarter, mainly due to an economic slowdown, pushing net profit in the period down to 2.46 bilion crowns from 3.51 billion.
The company is also likely to get a hit from the recent weakening of the Czech crown as it services an extensive foreign currency-denominated debt.
"The development of demand in the second half and the exchange rate of the crown will be decisive for (CEZ) profit," said Miroslava Cermakova from Atlantik FT.
"(CEZ) has approximately 10 billion crowns in foreign debt, for most of which it would have to create reserves to cover exchange rate losses," she told Reuters.
The crown lost about 10 percent of its value in May and June as it came under speculative attacks, but it has since recovered some of the losses.
The state, which holds a two-thirds stake, killed a proposal by CEZ's board to pay out a first-ever dividend on 1996 earnings, prompting analysts to say state ownership was raising investment risk.
"The current state owenrship is counterproductive, because the state as an owner is directed by macroeconomic thoughts, as the dividend case showed," said Michal Kusak of brokerage AKRO Capital.
Analysts said a government plan to separate the high-voltage national grid from CEZ by the end of the century would hurt the firm, and open the sector to competitors.
CEZ is still striving to finish a Soviet designed nuclear power plant at Temelin in the southern Czech Republic.
The opening date of the first the two rectors has been postponed a number of times, while costs of the project continue to rise. The latest opening date is 1999.
Costs of the nuclear power plant, which enviromentalists distrust as well as the government of neighbouring Austria, have risen to the currently forecasted 76 billion crowns.
Privatisation of the 67 percent state-stake in CEZ would be bright news for investors, but government officials have said this would be on the agenda only after Temelin is finished.
